title: Correcting Visual Blur Induced by Attention Distraction to Reduce Hallucinations: Algorithm and Theory
claim: Dispersed and fading attention causes hallucinations; our two-stage correction concentrates and reinforces visual attention during decoding.
layout: 4 panels: problems left, solutions right, bottom fusion strip with legend
description: A composite figure with a problem column on the left and a method column on the right. Top-left, Problem 1 shows a distracted cartoon person with dashed arrows to a sleeping cat, a car and a tree, leading to a hallucinated cat on wheels. Bottom-left, Problem 2 shows a text-token sequence ('The image shows ... lying on car') above three progressively blurrier cat photos, with the inequality VAR(t1)>VAR(t2)>VAR(t3). Top-right, Head-Level Attention Distraction Correction shows stacked heads with top-k selection, a bar chart of μ±σ, and the formula Δ1 = Avg − αVar. Middle-right, Dynamic Historical Attention Enhancement shows tokens, a history-retrieval arrow, an attention memory block, and Δ2 = γ·Historical Visual Attn. A bottom strip shows a gating module and the corrected attention grid, with a legend. Orange and yellow dominate, with blue dashed boxes.
caption: Motivation illustration and overview of AFIP.
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) frequently suffer from object hallucinations, yet the visual perceptual mechanism underlying this failure remains poorly understood. In this work, we reveal that hallucinations are strongly associated with a human-like attention distraction phenomenon, where humans under divided focus experience degraded visual clarity and produce inaccurate descriptions, while in models the same mechanism manifests as spatial inconsistency in multi-head attention and temporal fading of attention to image tokens during decoding. We further provide theoretical insights that attention dispersion increases model complexity and degrades classification generalization. Motivated by these findings, we propose an Attention-Focused Approach for Improved Image Perception (AFIP), which corrects attention distraction via cross-head attention enrichment and reinforces visual grounding through dynamic historical attention enhancement. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks and models validate the effectiveness of AFIP without additional training. Code is available at: https://github.com/MIKUZ12/AFIP.
